# I Learned to Touch-Type at 41, and It Was Humiliating

For about twenty years I typed with four fingers and a lot of confidence. I was fast, in the way a man hunting through a drawer for a pair of scissors is fast. Eyes down, two index fingers darting, the occasional thumb joining in for the space bar. I wrote reports, emails and one unfinished novel this way. I was fine with it.

Then last spring a colleague sat next to me while I was drafting something, watched for about a minute and said, kindly, "Do you want me to look away?"

That was it. I signed up for a course that evening.

## The first week is a punishment

Let me be honest about the start, because nobody warns you. When you begin touch-typing properly, you get slower. Dramatically slower. I went from roughly 45 words per minute to about 12. Twelve! My nephew, who is nine, types faster than that when he is texting his friends under the dinner table.

The method is simple enough. Your fingers rest on the "home row": A, S, D, F for the left hand, J, K, L and the semicolon for the right. Every key has a finger assigned to it. You do not look at the keyboard. You do not cheat. When you make a mistake, you correct it with the correct finger instead of reaching for the nearest one.

For the first few days, my brain felt like it was walking through wet cement. I knew where the letter E was, in the abstract. I simply could not make my left middle finger go there without a committee meeting.

## What actually helped

**Short sessions beat heroic ones.** I tried an hour on the second evening and ended up with stiff wrists and a grim mood. After that I did fifteen minutes each morning, before opening email. That was the habit that stuck. By day ten, fifteen minutes felt almost pleasant.

**Covering the keyboard felt silly but worked.** I draped a tea towel over my hands for the first month. Part of me felt like a nineteenth-century séance medium. But it forced me to stop peeking, and peeking is the thing that keeps you stuck.

**Accuracy before speed. Always.** The courses all say this, and I rolled my eyes, and then I proved them right. Whenever I pushed for speed, my errors spiked, and correcting errors wastes more time than typing slowly ever does. Once I let myself go at a comfortable crawl, the speed arrived on its own.

**Real words, not drills, eventually.** The early exercises are a stream of nonsense: "fjfj dkdk". It is useful for about a week. After that, I switched to typing out paragraphs from books I liked, which was far more bearable. I also used a free typing site that tracks which letters trip you up, and it turned out that my weakness was the letter Q, plus anything on the bottom row. Of course it was.

## The plateau nobody mentions

Around week five I hit a wall. My speed sat at 28 words per minute for what felt like a fortnight. I was typing correctly, mostly, and nothing improved. I nearly gave up and went back to my four-finger method, which at that point was faster.

What got me through was a piece of advice from a former secretary I know. She told me, "Your fingers are learning something your brain cannot see. Be patient with the part of you that is not conscious."

She was right. One morning in week seven I noticed I had been typing a sentence while thinking about what to have for lunch, and my hands had simply carried on. That moment is difficult to describe if you have not had it. It is a bit like realising you can ride a bike without thinking about balance.

## Where I am now

Three months in, I type at around 62 words per minute with decent accuracy. That is not spectacular. A professional transcriptionist would yawn. But it is nearly half again as fast as before, and, more importantly, I now look at the screen instead of the keys. I catch typos as they appear. My neck no longer hurts at the end of the workday, which I had assumed was simply what office jobs do to a person.

I also write more. This surprised me. When typing stopped being work, putting thoughts into sentences became less of a chore. This blog post, which would once have taken me an hour and a half, took about forty minutes.

## If you are thinking about it

A few quick thoughts for anyone considering the same thing:

1. **Pick a layout and stay with it.** If you use QWERTY, learn QWERTY. Do not switch to some exotic alternative in the middle of this.
2. **Check your posture.** Wrists straight, elbows around ninety degrees, screen at eye level. A cheap laptop stand and an external keyboard did more for me than any tip about finger technique.
3. **Expect a dip.** It is normal and it is temporary. If you are only going to try this once, do it during a quiet month at work, not the week of a big deadline.
4. **Keep your old method as a fallback.** I allowed myself to cheat when something was truly urgent. It slowed my progress slightly but kept me from resenting the whole project.

It is not too late. I am forty-one, my fingers are not young, and I managed it. If the idea has been nagging at you for years, as it nagged me, that is probably your answer.

Now, if you will excuse me, I have an unfinished novel to get back to. I might be able to finish it before I am fifty.
